mcqs.question: Why can't you generally prevent deadlock by eliminating mutual exclusion for a bank account balance field that multiple threads update?
options: Because mutual exclusion is required by law for financial systems specifically
Because bank account updates are always read-only operations
Because exclusive access is required for correctness there — concurrent unsynchronized writes would corrupt the balance, so removing exclusion isn't an available option
Because mutual exclusion can only be removed for resources with more than one instance
mcqs.explanation: Some resources are inherently exclusive by correctness requirement, not by arbitrary design choice — a mutable balance updated by concurrent writers needs exclusion to avoid corruption, so this attack point simply doesn't apply. It isn't a legal requirement or tied to instance count; it's about whether the resource can be safely shared at all.

mcqs.question: Why is attacking the no-preemption condition a poor fit for a physical printer mid-print, but a reasonable fit for CPU registers during a context switch?
options: Preemption is always safe for both — there's no meaningful difference
A printer's physical state can't be cleanly saved and resumed mid-page, while CPU register state can be saved and restored exactly, making preemption destructive for one and lossless for the other
CPU registers can never actually be preempted, only simulated
Printers are always preemptible in modern operating systems
mcqs.explanation: Preemption only works cleanly when the resource's state can be saved and restored without loss — which is exactly what a context switch does for registers. A printer mid-physical-print has no equivalent clean save/restore, so forcibly taking it back is destructive, not just costly.

mcqs.question: Why does enforcing a global, fixed lock-acquisition order across a codebase make circular wait structurally impossible?
options: It doesn't eliminate circular wait, only reduces its likelihood

Because a cycle would require some process to hold a higher-ranked lock while waiting for a lower-ranked one, which the ordering rule forbids by construction — so the resulting wait-for graph can never form a loop
Because it eliminates mutual exclusion between the locks
Because it guarantees only one thread ever runs at a time
mcqs.explanation: A cycle requires waiting to flow both 'forward' and 'backward' through the lock order at some point; forbidding acquisition against the fixed order makes that impossible to construct, ruling out circular wait entirely, not just making it less likely. It doesn't touch mutual exclusion or serialize all execution.

mcqs.question: Given the trade-offs across all four prevention strategies, which is generally the most broadly practical default for application code you fully control?
options: Attacking hold-and-wait via upfront resource acquisition, since it's simplest to reason about
Attacking mutual exclusion, since removing locks entirely is always safe
Attacking no-preemption via forced rollback, since it requires no code discipline
Attacking circular wait via global lock ordering, since it doesn't require advance knowledge of resource needs or resources being preemptible
mcqs.explanation: Global lock ordering is broadly applicable and cheap at runtime, needing only consistent discipline rather than advance resource knowledge (unlike hold-and-wait attacks) or preemptible resources (unlike no-preemption attacks). Removing mutual exclusion is unsafe wherever exclusivity is required for correctness — it is not 'always safe.'

mcqs.question: A team enforces lock ordering everywhere except in one rarely-executed error-handling branch, which acquires the same two locks in reverse order. What's the practical consequence?
options: None, since lock ordering only needs to hold in the common, frequently-executed paths
The system deadlocks immediately and constantly, making the bug obvious in testing
The single violation reintroduces circular wait exactly as if no ordering rule existed, and because the branch is rare, the resulting deadlock may only surface rarely in production
The runtime automatically detects and corrects the ordering violation
mcqs.explanation: Lock ordering is an all-or-nothing guarantee — a single code path violating it reintroduces the possibility of circular wait, regardless of how rarely that path executes. Rare paths are exactly what make these bugs hard to catch in testing and prone to surfacing only under real production conditions; nothing detects or fixes this automatically without dedicated tooling.
